### guardduty-finding-categories

**Claim.** GuardDuty detection categories include reconnaissance, instance compromise (for example cryptocurrency mining or communication with a known malicious IP), account compromise (for example API calls from an unusual geolocation or attempts to deactivate CloudTrail logging), bucket compromise, malware (in EC2 instances, container workloads, S3 uploads or AWS Backup data) and container compromise.

> "Instance compromise: Activity indicating an instance compromise, such as cryptocurrency mining, malware using domain generation algorithms (DGAs), outbound denial of service activity, an unusually high volume of network traffic, unusual network protocols, outbound instance communication with a known malicious IP, temporary Amazon EC2 credentials used by an external IP address, and data exfiltration using DNS."
> — [Intelligent Threat Detection – Amazon GuardDuty FAQs – Amazon Web Services](https://aws.amazon.com/guardduty/faqs/)

> "Account compromise: Common patterns indicative of account compromise, including API calls from an unusual geolocation or anonymizing proxy, attempts to deactivate CloudTrail logging, unusual instance or infrastructure launches, infrastructure deployments in an unusual region, the exfiltration of credentials, suspicious database login activity, and API calls from known malicious IP addresses."
> — [Intelligent Threat Detection – Amazon GuardDuty FAQs – Amazon Web Services](https://aws.amazon.com/guardduty/faqs/)

> "Bucket compromise: Activity indicating a bucket compromise, such as suspicious data access patterns indicating credential misuse, unusual Amazon S3 API activity from a remote host, unauthorized Amazon S3 access from known malicious IP addresses, and API calls to retrieve data in Amazon S3 buckets from a user that had no prior history of accessing the bucket or invoked from an unusual location."
> — [Intelligent Threat Detection – Amazon GuardDuty FAQs – Amazon Web Services](https://aws.amazon.com/guardduty/faqs/)

> "Malware: GuardDuty can detect the presence of malware—such as trojans, worms, crypto miners, rootkits, or bots—that may be used to compromise your Amazon EC2 instance or container workloads, or that is uploaded to your Amazon S3 buckets or that exists in your AWS Backup data."
> — [Intelligent Threat Detection – Amazon GuardDuty FAQs – Amazon Web Services](https://aws.amazon.com/guardduty/faqs/)

> "Container compromise: Activity identifying possible malicious or suspicious behavior in container workloads is detected by continuously monitoring and profiling Amazon EKS clusters by analyzing its Amazon EKS audit logs and container runtime activity in Amazon EKS or Amazon ECS."

**Scope.** per monitored resource type.

> "Runtime Monitoring uses a GuardDuty security agent that adds visibility into runtime behavior, such as file access, process execution, command line arguments, and network connections. For each resource type that you want to monitor for potential threats, you can manage the security agent for that specific resource type either automatically or manually (with an exception to Fargate (Amazon ECS only)). Managing the security agent automatically means that you permit GuardDuty to install and update the security agent on your behalf."

> "For GuardDuty to receive these runtime events, you must use the Automated agent configuration."

### guardduty-sra-export-findings-log-archive

**Claim.** In the AWS Security Reference Architecture, GuardDuty is enabled in all accounts through AWS Organizations, findings are managed in the delegated administrator (Security Tooling) account, and active findings are exported to a central S3 bucket in the Log Archive account, encrypted with a KMS customer managed key, so they are retained beyond 90 days.

**Write it as.** `enabled in all accounts through AWS Organizations` · `exported to a central S3 bucket in the Log Archive account` · `retain the findings beyond 90 days`

**Scope.** per organization (reference architecture).

> "In the AWS SRA, GuardDuty is enabled in all accounts through AWS Organizations, and all findings are viewable and actionable by appropriate security teams in the GuardDuty delegated administrator account (in this case, the Security Tooling account). GuardDuty active findings are exported to a central S3 bucket in the Log Archive account, so you can retain the findings beyond 90 days."
> — [Security OU – Security Tooling account](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/security-reference-architecture/security-tooling.html)

> "The findings in the bucket S3 are encrypted with an AWS KMS customer managed key."
> — [Security OU – Security Tooling account](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/security-reference-architecture/security-tooling.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-12.

### guardduty-suppression-rule-still-generates

**Claim.** Suppression rules suppress findings that match specific combinations of attributes, for example by automatically archiving matching port scan findings, but GuardDuty still generates all findings and keeps a complete and immutable history of all activity; suppression rules defined in the GuardDuty administrator account apply to member accounts, which can't modify them.

**Write it as.** `GuardDuty still generates all findings` · `GuardDuty member accounts can't modify suppression rules`

> "With suppression rules, GuardDuty still generates all findings. Suppression rules provide suppression of findings while maintaining a complete and immutable history of all activity."
> — [Concepts and key terms in Amazon GuardDuty](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/guardduty_concepts.html)

> "Suppression rules defined in the GuardDuty administrator account apply to the GuardDuty member accounts. GuardDuty member accounts can't modify suppression rules."
> — [Concepts and key terms in Amazon GuardDuty](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/guardduty_concepts.html)

> "Suppression rules allow you to create very specific combinations of attributes to suppress findings."
> — [Concepts and key terms in Amazon GuardDuty](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/guardduty_concepts.html)

> "This rule would result in port scan findings being automatically archived from the instances that meet the criteria."
> — [Concepts and key terms in Amazon GuardDuty](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/guardduty_concepts.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-12.

### guardduty-suspend-keeps-findings

**Claim.** If you suspend GuardDuty, it stops monitoring and generating new findings, but existing findings remain intact, you are not charged for using GuardDuty while it is suspended, and you can re-enable it later. Suspending does not change protected buckets under Malware Protection for S3, and the account keeps incurring Malware Protection for S3 usage costs.

**Write it as.** `Your existing findings remain intact` · `You don't get charged for using GuardDuty`

**Scope.** Malware Protection for S3 protected buckets keep incurring cost.

> "If you suspend GuardDuty, it no longer monitors the security of your AWS environment or generates new findings. Your existing findings remain intact and are not affected by the GuardDuty suspension. You can choose to re-enable GuardDuty later."
> — [Suspending or disabling GuardDuty](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/guardduty_suspend-disable.html)

> "You don't get charged for using GuardDuty when the service is suspended."
> — [Suspending or disabling GuardDuty](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/guardduty_suspend-disable.html)

> "If you have enabled Malware Protection for S3 for one or more protected buckets in your account, then suspending or disabling GuardDuty doesn't impact the status of a protected bucket under Malware Protection for S3. Even after suspending or disabling GuardDuty, your account will continue incurring the usage costs associated with the Malware Protection for S3 feature."
> — [Suspending or disabling GuardDuty](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/guardduty_suspend-disable.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-12.
